q: Should I really hack my Switch 2?
a: Let's be responsible here. If you don't know what you're doing, what you expect to gain from it, or the risks involved, you should probably stay away from these hacking methods. They are currently quite limited, so only proceed if you fully understand where things stand today:

Barely useful: There are very few genuinely cool things you can actually do with it as of today, and you can count them on one hand. On top of that, it's currently only possible with a game that isn't available anywhere.

Barely successful: Even in perfect conditions as of today, such as Ethernet, no SD card, and a single account, you may need several attempts, and it is not reliable. It will always be tethered to a PC, and it's only really doable if you have an app that is basically unavailable everywhere.

Slightly risky: There is always a chance of your console getting banned, locking you out of game updates, DLCs, game key cards, and many other benefits. It can also get bricked, and there is no way to back up or restore your NAND if that happens.

So if, after all of that, you still want to do it, that's up to you. There is a lot of development going on, and things can change over time and will probably get better. Just make sure you fully understand the risks and limitations before proceeding.

Everyone is vagueposting: everyone has magical solutions, everything is solved, an amazing series of achievements, and so on. But until someone publishes something that you, as a beginner, can actually follow and use to achieve something, it's still vagueposting, and you should treat it as such.

q: I have two Switch 2s and I want to keep one untouched and the other just for tinkering/JB. What should I do?
a: The recommended path is to keep one Switch 2 completely untouched for regular use, which is great.

For the other Switch 2, before proceeding with anything, load all your virtual game cards and download as many games as you think you'll use, so it's in a state you're happy with. Then, after making sure you have an exploitable game or app, either digitally or physically, you can set up 90dns, which will disconnect your console from Nintendo's servers (How to set up 90dns). Once that's done, you can unlink this console from Nintendo's website. This allows you to use your games and virtual game cards on your untouched console while preserving everything on the 90dns-configured one that you'll use for tinkering with exploits.

If you ever connect the tinkering console without 90dns, it may communicate with Nintendo's servers, potentially causing unwanted telemetry, loss of your games, forced updates, a banned console, or other undesired consequences. Always keep that in mind.
Also, after unlinking a console, you cannot do this process again unless one full year has passed, so plan accordingly.

q: How does this work?
a: Basically, we run arbitrary code on the console to trigger a vulnerability that allows privilege escalation by giving our process PID 1. That's cool because every process with a PID ≤ 6 has elevated privileges, and we can manipulate it to our advantage.

A payload starts an RPC server, which lets a server PC make a series of native calls to the console. This effectively gives it control over various system functions and enables the actions described above.

q: What do tethered, untethered, semi-tethered, and semi-untethered mean?
a: These terms describe how long an exploit survives a reboot and what is needed to re-enable it.

Tethered: the exploit has to be applied again after every reboot using an external device, such as a PC or dongle. Without that device, you either cannot boot into the modified state or cannot use the exploit at all.
Semi-tethered: the console boots and works normally without the exploit, but you still need the external device to re-enable it after each reboot.
Semi-untethered: the console boots normally, and after a reboot you re-enable the exploit with a small on-console step, such as launching an app. No external device is required.
Untethered: the exploit persists across reboots. There is no re-enable step and no PC or external device needed after the initial setup.

All currently available Switch 2 exploits are tethered and require a PC to trigger them. After a reboot you have to launch the game entrypoint and run the PC-side tools again. The console itself still boots normally as a stock console, so in the stricter console-jailbreak sense it is closer to semi-tethered, but the exploit does not survive a reboot and is not untethered.

q: Should I use 90dns to block connections to Nintendo?
a: Yes, you probably should. That way, no telemetry or unwanted connections to Nintendo's servers will occur while you are using the payloads. The console may nag you, preventing you from using some features like the embedded browser, but you probably won't need it for our purposes anyway.

q: Can I do this in Airplane Mode?
a: No, you can't. The payloads require a local network connection to run because a PC on the network does all the work to achieve escalation.

q: Can I update my console while using this?
a: No, you shouldn't. Updating your console might patch the vulnerabilities used by the payloads, rendering them ineffective. Firmware 23.5.0 is now out and is expected to patch some or all of the current entry points, so stay on 23.0.1 for now if you want to keep the current exploits.

There are a lot of announcements around, but much of the work is not published, and some of it may never be released. So don't get too excited; wait until something is actually usable before relying on it.

q: Do I need to update my modded Switch 1 to transfer the save?
a: Yes, because you need to log in with the same account as your Switch 2, and it will ask for an update to proceed. The transfer process happens locally, but the authentication requires a connection to Nintendo, so you cannot even have 90dns set.

q: Can I transfer the save through NSO by uploading it to the cloud?
a: Yes, you can, but we don't know if this can cause problems in the future.

a: Technically yes, but you need a fully exploitable app to gain the privileges required to run saves. If you already have one, why bother? Still, you can use ns2-savekit to inject the modded save.

q: Is there a risk of ban for using this?
a: Of course, there is always a risk. It's not guaranteed, but who knows. People usually don't get banned immediately; they get flagged, and eventually a wave of bans happens all at once. So be cautious and understand the potential consequences before proceeding.

Usually accounts don't get banned unless you cheat in online games. But consoles do get banned if they are detected running unauthorized software or exploits through telemetry. This will lock you out of accessing any online services, including game updates and DLCs — only firmware updates pass through a ban.

q: What does being nagged mean?
a: Nagging can mean two things:
1. Being unable to use certain features or the system itself until you address the nag, such as updating the console or connecting to the internet for verification.
2. Receiving persistent notifications or prompts that require your attention, which can be annoying and disruptive to your experience.

q: What is the difference between nag, supernag, and ultranag?
a: Nag (normal update nag): the standard system-update prompt. It usually has three options and can typically be cleared by powering the console off and booting into maintenance mode, which deletes the downloaded update data.

Supernag: a persistent update prompt seen historically on Switch 1. It usually has two options, cannot be cleared through maintenance mode, and is tied to an update record or system save. It was often triggered by connecting to Nintendo's servers on older firmware, or by 90DNS not fully blocking a connection. It is not the same as the Switch 2 ultranag.

Ultranag: the mechanism added around system update 21.x on Switch and Switch 2. When the console's update-check state is update_needed or network_error, Webkit-based features show “This feature is not available.” Non-captive Webkit features such as the eShop also lock if there has not been a successful update check in 24 hours. 90DNS does not cause it, but it makes it apply to the captive portal too. It does not block the game entrypoints used for payloads.
tl;dr: nag is the normal update prompt, supernag is the older and harder-to-clear update prompt on Switch 1, and ultranag is the Switch 2-era Webkit lockout tied to the console's update-check state.
You can read the technical details in the 90DNS documentation.

q: How can I prevent nagging?
a: To prevent the nag, either keep your console up to date and avoid DNS blocking of the URL https://bvc.p01.lp1.bvc.srv.nintendo.net (which 90dns would block), so it can reach the necessary servers for verification and updates. Alternatively, keep the console in airplane mode or disconnected from any network so it never checks at all, but then you won't be able to use exploits that require local network access.

q: How do I know if I'm nagged?
a: Disable 90dns, then try to open the eShop. If you see a message with no error code that simply says "This feature is not available.", your console is in the ultranag state described above.

q: How do I know if I'm banned?
a: Disable 90dns, then try to open the eShop. If you see an error message with code 2124-4007 or 2124-4508, your console is banned.

q: Will I be able to play new games on my "hacked" console?
a: Games that support 23.0.1 will work and run just fine, but any new games that require a later version will not be playable on your "hacked" console while it stays on that firmware. Now that 23.5.0 is out, 23.0.1 is the previous version, but it remains the one to stay on if you want to keep the current exploits. So don't get your hopes up too much; we just have to wait. Maybe some solution will come up eventually.

q: Will we be able to play or dump games from future versions?
a: Probably not for games that require a later firmware. The same logic applies to running, reading, and dumping: the console cannot run or decrypt content that is not compatible with its firmware version unless it is updated. But if the games were made for 23.0.1 or lower, then you can play and dump them, since there is no restriction preventing you from running those games on your 23.0.1 console. And if the exploit is patched in a newer firmware, how would you dump or play games that require it?

q: Do we know when a new firmware update will come out?
a: Firmware 23.5.0 is already out. The recommendation is not to update to it, since it is expected to patch some or all of the current entry points. Stay on 23.0.1 and keep 90dns enabled to prevent forced updates. More updates will eventually arrive, but the advice is the same: stay blocked until new research is available.

q: Now that FS is patched for 23.5.0 and upwards, does this mean it's patched for all entrypoints?
a: FS itself, or the method for privileged escalation, is patched. But our way of running arbitrary code through the entrypoints is in many cases still possible, which may allow us to keep investigating new breaking points for elevation in the future.
Even though new payloads that use FS for escalation might only work on 23.0.1, new developments might still appear eventually.

q: Any settings I should change to be ready?
a: Sure. Make sure to disable sending error logs (Share Error Information OFF) and automatic updates (Software Auto-Updates OFF) in your console's System Settings (Settings > System).

Also, if you use 90dns, make sure to disable IPv6 in your console's network settings so it doesn't use automatic DNS settings that could bypass 90dns. If you have an active NSO subscription, remember to disable cloud saves as well.

q: Why don't we have payloads for most other games yet?
a: Wow, they're kinda hard to develop. You need to understand the game's architecture and functionality and take advantage of it.

Also, all of them are different: some are written in Lua, others in JavaScript, and the original one in BASIC, making them difficult to port or support with a universal solution. You'll just have to wait for someone to take the time to develop a compatible solution for each specific game.

q: Is Switch 2 emulation real?
a: Yes, absolutely, and it is advancing pretty fast. But everyone is doing their own fork instead of focusing on one thing, so there are a lot of versions out there, and some are of unknown provenance and could be unsafe, so be careful and check what you're using.
You will find some that run certain things better than others, while others are near-duplicate forks of the original work.

q: I already have one exploitable game. Do I need another one?
a: No, I mean, it's cool if you have it; some will advance more quickly, of course. But you don't necessarily need another one to benefit from the exploit, and ports will probably come to support your existing game.

If you have any of the supported Artemis Engine demos (Seedsow, Nora, Hamidashi) with your modded save, you can rest easy. If you have SmileBasic 4, then you can be proud because you're ready. CIV and Balatro are too recent, so we don't know, but they might get support in the future.

q: How can I improve my chances of getting FS with SmileBasic 4?
a: The process is extremely time-sensitive, so it's normal not to get it after a few tries.
What you can do (and what is normally recommended) is connect your Switch via Ethernet to reduce network latency and improve your chances of success.
Additionally, some users report that removing the SD card improves the chances of success, and having only one user profile on the system can also help.
